newsitem.title: USA: HORSE RACING-"NEW PLAYER" BUYS $1.5 MILLION SALES TOPPER.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-"NEW PLAYER" BUYS $1.5 MILLION SALES TOPPER.

text.p: A colt sired by Storm Cat was the $1.5 million sales topper at Keeneland's July Selected Yearling Sale Tuesday.

Bob Baffert, trainer of Silver Charm, this year's Kentucky Derby and Preakness winner, picked out and bought the colt for a still-undisclosed American buyer. "A new player" in the market was all Baffert could say.
Americans have generally felt shut out of the world's most expensive yearling sale in recent years by flowing Arabian petrodollars, Japanese yen, British and Irish pounds.

"He was watching the Silver Charm stuff," said Boffert of his new client, "and wanted to get involved. He wanted a horse to take to the Derby. He called me on Sunday -- I've never met him -- and asked me to pick out a horse."

Boffert was on the phone with the buyer throughout the tense sale "and I lost him at $600,000. I called him back. I didn't know if he wanted me to bid beyond $1 million but he was a game guy and said 'don't let him go.'"
The underbidder was owner Bob Lewis and his agent D.Wayne Lukas. Boffert trains Lewis' star Silver Charm,
"The colt's value will be peanuts compared to what I paid today," predicted Boffert.
Numerous Japanese buyers, British agents for the royal Dubai Maktoum brothers' British and Dubai facilities, and Irish agent Demi O'Byrne were the most active in both sale sessions.
"Cot" Campbell, who started the sucessful Dogwood Stables, the first American syndicate in 1971, bought two horses but said: "It's hard for a guy like me to participate.
"It used to be some of the yearlings would fall through the cracks, but now the pinhooks (bargain-hunters buying not to own but to resell) are there to gobble them up."
Like most American buyers, Campbell said, "I can't afford to play the $600,000 to $700,000 market." He will pursue the September sales for better buys.

High prices do not guarantee winning horses. "Only time will tell if they're any good or not," said O'Byrne of his aggressive purchases for Michael Tabor and John Magnier, owner of Coolmore Stud in Ireland.
Keeneland provided Japanese language translators for the sales, and served sushi, along with tuna salad.
The auction showcased yearlings by world-famous sires like Mr. Prospector, Danzig, A.P. Indy, Storm Cat, Gone West, Seeking the Gold and Seattle Slew.
Sale official said 175 head were sold, the gross amount was $62,565,000, the average was $357,514 compared to last year's $349,880 and the median price for both years was $300,000.
The average price this year was up 2.2 percent and total sales were up 7.1 percent.
